P000002T1T_1Predicate

Given any two distinct points, each has a neighborhood not containing the other point.

Equivalently, any of the following equivalent properties holds:

  • Points are closed in XX (that is, for each x∈Xx\in X the singleton {x}\{x\} is closed).
  • Finite subspaces are Discrete.
  • Each point is an intersection of open sets.
  • Each point is an intersection of its neighborhoods.

See T1 space on Wikipedia for a more extensive list.

Defined on page 11 of Counterexamples in Topology.

Meta-properties

  • The Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) is T1T_1 iff XX is R0R_0.
  • This property is hereditary.

P000010SemiregularPredicate

A space with a base ℬ\mathcal{B} of regular open sets, that is, int⁡(cl⁡(O))=O\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{cl}(O)) = O for every O∈ℬO \in \mathcal{B}.

Defined in 14E of General Topology (Willard).

  • This property is hereditary with respect to open sets.
  • This property is not hereditary with respect to closed sets (Example: Excluded Point Topology on a Three-Point Set · Semiregular and Sierpinski space · Semiregular.)

P000011RegularPredicate

A space in which a closed set and a point not contained in it can be separated by open neighborhoods. In other words, given a closed set AA and a point b∉Ab \notin A, there are disjoint open sets OAO_A and ObO_b containing AA and bb, respectively.

Equivalently, every point has a neighborhood base consisting of closed sets.

See Definition 14.1 and Theorem 14.3 in General Topology (Willard).

Meta-properties

  • This property is hereditary.
  • XX is Regular iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) is T3T_3.

P000012Completely regularPredicate

A space in which points and closed sets can be separated by a function. Namely, given a closed set AA and a point b∉Ab \notin A, there is a continuous function f:X→[0,1]f:X \rightarrow [0,1] such that f(A)={0}f(A) = \{0\} and f(b)=1f(b)=1.

Equivalently, the cozero sets form a base for the topology.

Defined in 14.8 of General Topology (Willard).

Equivalently, the topology is induced by a uniformity. See Theorem 38.2 in General Topology (Willard) and Uniform space on Wikipedia.

Meta-properties

  • XX is Completely regular iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) is T312T_{3 \frac{1}{2}}.
  • This property is hereditary.
  • This property is preserved by arbitrary products.

Sources cited by Pi-Base

P000015Perfectly normalPredicate

For any disjoint closed sets AA and BB in XX, there is a continuous function f:X→[0,1]f: X \rightarrow [0,1] such that f−1({0})=Af^{-1}(\{0\}) = A and f−1({1})=Bf^{-1}(\{1\}) = B.

This is equivalent to each of the following:

  • XX is Normal and a GδG_\delta space (i.e., every closed set is a GδG_\delta set).

  • Every closed set in XX is a zero set (i.e., f−1(0)f^{-1}(0) for some continuous f:X→[0,1]f:X\to[0,1]).

  • Every open set in XX is a cozero set (i.e., f−1((0,1])f^{-1}((0,1]) for some continuous f:X→[0,1]f:X\to[0,1]).

The equivalence between these conditions (Vedenissoff's theorem) is shown for example in Theorem 1.5.19 of General Topology (Engelking, 1989) (under the assumption of a T1T_1 space, but the proof does not use that assumption). See also Why are these two definitions of a perfectly normal space equivalent?.

Defined on page 16 of Counterexamples in Topology (as perfectly T4T_4).

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is hereditary (see Theorem 2.1.6 in General Topology (Engelking, 1989)).

Sources cited by Pi-Base

  • Counterexamples in Topology
  • General Topology (Engelking, 1989)
  • Why are these two definitions of a perfectly normal space equivalent?

P000016CompactPredicate

Every open cover of the space has a finite subcover.

Equivalently, every open cover of the space has an [open] finite refinement.

Defined on page 18 of Counterexamples in Topology.

Some authors call this property "quasi-compact", and use "compact" to mean quasi-compact and T2T_2.

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is hereditary with respect to closed sets.
  • This property is preserved by finite disjoint unions.
  • This property is preserved by arbitrary products. (Tychonoff's theorem)
  • This property is preserved in any coarser topology.

P000019Countably compactPredicate

Every countable open cover of XX has a finite subcover.

Equivalently, every infinite set in XX has an ω\omega-accumulation point in XX.

Equivalently, every sequence in XX has an accumulation point in XX (that is, a point such that each of its neighborhoods contains infinitely many terms of the sequence).

Defined on page 19 of Counterexamples in Topology. See for example Countably compact space on Wikipedia for a proof of the equivalences above.

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is hereditary with respect to closed sets.

P000034Fully normalPredicate

Every open cover of XX is normal.

This is equivalent to each of the following:

  • Every open cover has an open star-refinement.

  • Every open cover has an open barycentric refinement.

  • Every open cover has a subordinate partition of unity.

  • Every open cover has a locally finite subordinate partition of unity.

  • XX is Normal and Paracompact.

The star St(A,ℬ)\text{St}(A, \mathcal{B}) for A⊆XA\subseteq X and ℬ\mathcal{B} a family of subsets of XX, is the set ⋃{B∈ℬ:B∩A≠∅}\bigcup\{B\in \mathcal{B} : B\cap A\neq\emptyset\}. We say 𝒱\mathcal{V} is a star-refinement of 𝒰\mathcal{U} if 𝒱∗={St(V,𝒱):V∈𝒱}\mathcal{V}^\ast = \{\text{St}(V, \mathcal{V}): V\in\mathcal{V}\} is a refinement of 𝒰\mathcal{U}. We say 𝒱\mathcal{V} is a barycentric refinement of 𝒰\mathcal{U} if 𝒱Δ={St(x,𝒱):x∈X}\mathcal{V}^\Delta = \{\text{St}(x, \mathcal{V}): x\in X\} is a refinement of 𝒰\mathcal{U}. We say 𝒰\mathcal{U} is a normal cover if there exists a sequence of open covers (𝒰n)(\mathcal{U}_n) such that 𝒰=𝒰1\mathcal U=\mathcal U_1 and each 𝒰n+1\mathcal{U}_{n+1} is a star-refinement of 𝒰n\mathcal{U}_n. We say that a family of functions (fi)(f_i) is a partition of unity if the fi:X→[0,1]f_i:X\to [0, 1] are continuous and ∑ifi=1\sum_i f_i = 1. Here (∑ifi)(x)=∑ifi(x)(\sum_i f_i)(x) = \sum_i f_i(x) is defined as supremum over finite sums fi1(x)+⋯+fik(x)f_{i_1}(x)+ \dots +f_{i_k}(x). We say that a partition of unity (fi)(f_i) is subordinate to a cover (Ui)(U_i) of XX if {x∈X:fi(x)>0}⊆Ui\{x\in X : f_i(x) > 0\}\subseteq U_i for all ii. We say that a partition of unity (fi)(f_i) is locally finite when the cover consisting of sets {x∈X:fi(x)>0}\{x\in X : f_i(x) > 0\} is locally finite.

See Answer to "Fully normal implies paracompact without a $T_1$ assumption?" for proof of the equivalences.

Also see Henno Brandsma: On paracompactness, full normality and the like (available here).

(Note: Counterexamples in Topology defines this property on page 23 as "fully T4T_4". Misleadingly, it also calls "star refinement" what all other major sources call a barycentric refinement.)

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.

P000038Injectively path connectedPredicate

P000041Locally connectedPredicate

The topology of XX has a base consisting of Connected open sets.

This is equivalent to each of the following:

  • The connected components of every open set are open.

  • XX is locally connected at xx for every x∈Xx\in X; that is, each xx has a neighborhood base consisting of open connected sets.

  • XX is connected im kleinen at xx for every x∈Xx\in X; that is, each xx has a neighborhood base consisting of (not necessarily open) connected sets.

Note: In general, local connectedness at a point xx is not equivalent to connectedness im kleinen at xx. But the corresponding global statements (where the condition holds at every point) are equivalent.

For terminology and the equivalence between the conditions above, see section 2 of The Mazurkiewicz distance and sets that are finitely connected at the boundary (Björn, Björn, Shanmugalingam) and Locally connected space on Wikipedia, plus the references therein.

Defined on page 30 of Counterexamples in Topology.

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is hereditary with respect to open sets.

P000042Locally path connectedPredicate

The topology of XX has a base consisting of Path connected open sets.

This is equivalent to each of the following:

  • The path components of every open set are open.

  • XX is locally path connected at xx for every x∈Xx\in X; that is, each xx has a neighborhood base consisting of open path connected sets.

  • XX is path connected im kleinen at xx for every x∈Xx\in X; that is, each xx has a neighborhood base consisting of (not necessarily open) path connected sets.

  • (LC0LC^0 = locally 00-connected) For each x∈Xx\in X, every neighborhood UU of xx contains a neighborhood VV of xx such that every continuous ϕ:S0→V\phi:S^0\to V is null-homotopic in UU (where S0={−1,1}S^0=\{-1,1\} with the discrete topology).

Note: In general, local path connectedness at a point xx is not equivalent to path connectedness im kleinen at xx. But the corresponding global statements (where the condition holds at every point) are equivalent.

For terminology and the equivalence between the conditions above, see section 2 of The Mazurkiewicz distance and sets that are finitely connected at the boundary (Björn, Björn, Shanmugalingam) and Locally connected space on Wikipedia, plus the references therein, and also Answer to "Definition of locally pathwise connected".

A set A⊆XA\subseteq X is called locally dense (or preopen) if every x∈Ax\in A has neighbourhood UU with U∩AU\cap A dense in UU (equivalently, A⊆int⁡(A‾)A\subseteq\operatorname{int}(\overline A)).

P000053MetrizablePredicate

The topology on the space XX is induced by some metric dd.

A metric is a function d:X×X→ℝd:X \times X \to \mathbb{R} such that for all x,y,z∈Xx,y,z \in X, (i) d(x,y)≥0d(x,y) \geq 0 and d(x,y)=0d(x,y)=0 if and only if x=yx=y; (ii) d(x,y)=d(y,x)d(x,y) = d(y,x); (iii) d(x,z)≤d(x,y)+d(y,z)d(x,z) \leq d(x,y) + d(y,z).

Given a metric dd and x∈Xx \in X, ϵ>0\epsilon>0, define B(x,ϵ)={y∈X:d(x,y)<ϵ}B(x,\epsilon) = \{y \in X: d(x,y)<\epsilon\}. Then the sets B(x,ϵ)B(x,\epsilon) form a base for a topology, called the topology induced by dd.

Defined on page 37 of Counterexamples in Topology.

Meta-properties

  • The Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) is Metrizable iff XX is Pseudometrizable.
  • This property is hereditary.

P000055Completely metrizablePredicate

The topology on the space XX is induced by some complete metric dd, that is, a metric for which every Cauchy sequence converges.

A sequence (xn)n(x_n)_n is Cauchy provided for each distance ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there is a natural number NN for which d(xi,xj)<ϵd(x_i,x_j)<\epsilon for all i,j>Ni,j>N.

Defined in 24.2 of General Topology (Willard). Called topologically complete on page 37 of Counterexamples in Topology; this last term has also been used for Čech complete and Dieudonné complete.

Meta-properties

P000061Cozero complementedPredicate

Every cozero set UU in XX has a cozero complement, that is, a cozero set VV disjoint from UU such that U∪VU\cup V is dense in XX.

A cozero set is a set of the form coz(f):={x∈X:f(x)≠0}\text{coz}(f):=\{x\in X:f(x)\ne 0\} for some continuous function f:X→ℝf:X\to\mathbb R; equivalently, the complement of a zero set.

Defined in Cozero complemented spaces; when the space of minimal prime ideals of a $C(X)$ is compact (Henriksen & Woods), with the additional usual assumption of T312T_{3 \frac{1}{2}}. We do not make that assumption here.

Note: For a T312T_{3 \frac{1}{2}} space, being cozero complemented is equivalent to various algebraic properties of the ring C(X)C(X) of continuous real-valued functions on XX. See Theorem 1.3 in Cozero complemented spaces; when the space of minimal prime ideals of a $C(X)$ is compact (Henriksen & Woods).

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is hereditary with respect to cozero sets (see Lemma 1.5(b) in Cozero complemented spaces; when the space of minimal prime ideals of a $C(X)$ is compact (Henriksen & Woods)), and in particular, with respect to clopen sets.
  • This property is preserved by arbitrary disjoint unions.

P000063Čech completePredicate

A T312T_{3 \frac{1}{2}} space XX that is a GδG_\delta set in some compactification of XX (equivalently, in every compactification of XX).

Equivalently, there is a sequence 𝒰1,𝒰2,…\mathcal{U}_1, \mathcal{U}_2, \dots of open covers of XX such that whenever ℱ\mathcal{F} is a family of closed sets with the finite intersection property and such that for each nn there is some Fn∈ℱF_n \in \mathcal{F} with Fn⊆UF_n \subseteq U for some U∈𝒰nU \in \mathcal{U}_n, then ⋂ℱ≠∅\bigcap \mathcal F \neq \emptyset.

See Section 3.9 ("Čech-complete spaces") of General Topology (Engelking, 1989), specifically Theorems 3.9.1 and 3.9.2 for the equivalences above.

Such spaces are called topologically complete in A characterization of topologically complete spaces in the sense of E. Čech in terms of convergence of functions. (Frolik, 1963); this last term has also been used for Completely metrizable and Dieudonné complete.

Meta-properties

  • This property is hereditary with respect to closed sets (see Theorem 3.9.6 in General Topology (Engelking, 1989)).
  • This property is hereditary with respect to GδG_\delta sets (see Theorem 3.9.6 in General Topology (Engelking, 1989)).

P000075SpectralPredicate

A Compact Sober space for which the collection of compact open subsets is closed under finite intersections and forms a base for the topology.

In the theory of Stone duality, for every bounded distributive lattice there exists a unique spectral space whose compact open subsets are order-isomorphic to that lattice and whose points are the prime ideals of the lattice. Additionally, spectra of commutative rings endowed with the Zariski topology are spectral spaces and vice versa, although this association is not one-to-one. For a comprehensive overview of this and other information on spectral spaces, see Spectral spaces (Dickmann, Schwartz, Tressl).

See example 21, section 2.6 of mr 1077251 and the section on Spectral spaces from the Stacks project.

P000076ProximalPredicate

A Completely regular space such that there exists a uniformity generating the topology of the space such that the entourage-picker has a winning strategy in Bell's proximal game introduced in An infinite game with topological consequences (Bell).

Equivalently, the entourage-picker has a winning strategy for this variation defined as Game 1.11 of Tactic-proximal compact spaces are strong Eberlein compact (Clontz): during round 00, the entourage-picker chooses an entourage D0D_0 of the diagonal from the Completely regular space's universal uniformity, and the point-picker chooses some point x0x_0. Then during round n+1n+1, the entourage-picker chooses an entourage Dn+1D_{n+1}, and the point-picker chooses some point xn+1∈Dn[xn]x_{n+1}\in D_n[x_n]. The entourage-picker wins provided that either the sequence xnx_n converges or the intersection ⋂n<ωDn[xn]\bigcap_{n<\omega}D_n[x_n] is empty.

Note that while many authors require Proximal spaces to be T2T_2 (equivalently, T0T_0), we do not require this separation axiom here. However, due to the first meta-property below, many results about T2T_2 Proximal spaces may be generalized by considering the Kolmogorov quotient.

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does. (Is a space proximal whenever its $T_0$ quotient is?)
  • This property is hereditary with respect to closed sets (see Lemma 7 in An infinite game with topological consequences (Bell)).
  • This property is preserved by Σ\Sigma-products (see Theorem 8 in An infinite game with topological consequences (Bell)).

Sources cited by Pi-Base

P000077Corson compactPredicate

XX is homeomorphic to a compact subspace of a Σ\Sigma-product of real lines. By homogeneity of the real line, one can assume the Σ\Sigma-product is of the form

Y={x=(xα)∈ℝΓ:{α:xα≠0} is countable}\quad Y=\{x=(x_\alpha)\in\mathbb R^\Gamma:\{\alpha:x_\alpha\ne 0\}\text{ is countable}\}

for some set Γ\Gamma. The space YY has the topology of pointwise convergence induced from the product topology of ℝΓ\mathbb R^\Gamma.

P000081Countably tightPredicate

XX has countable tightness: For each A⊆XA\subseteq X and each p∈A‾p\in \overline A there is a countable subset D⊆AD\subseteq A such that p∈D‾p\in \overline D.

Equivalently, XX is countably generated: For each A⊆XA\subseteq X, AA is closed whenever A∩CA\cap C is closed in CC for every countable C⊆XC\subseteq X (or the equivalent condition for open sets).

P000085Basically disconnectedPredicate

The closure of every cozero set in XX is open or, equivalently, clopen.

A cozero set is a set of the form {x∈X:f(x)>0}\{x\in X:f(x)>0\} for some continuous function f:X→ℝf:X\to\mathbb R; equivalently, the complement of a zero set.

Equivalently, any two disjoint open sets, at least one of which is a cozero set, have disjoint closures.

Defined in problem 1H of Rings of Continuous Functions (Gillman & Jerison).

P000088Collectionwise normalPredicate

For every discrete family (Fi)i∈I(F_i)_{i \in I} of closed subsets of XX, there exists a pairwise disjoint family of open sets (Ui)i∈I(U_i)_{i \in I} with Fi⊆UiF_i \subseteq U_i for all ii.

Equivalently, for every discrete family (Fi)i∈I(F_i)_{i \in I} of closed subsets of XX, there exists a discrete family of open sets (Ui)i∈I(U_i)_{i \in I} with Fi⊆UiF_i \subseteq U_i for all ii.

Terminology:

  • A discrete family is a family of subsets such that each point of XX has a neighborhood meeting at most one of the subsets.
  • In the first definition, the family of open sets (Ui)i(U_i)_i is sometimes called a disjoint open expansion of the family (Fi)i(F_i)_i.
  • In the second definition, the family of open sets (Ui)i(U_i)_i is sometimes called a discrete open expansion of the family (Fi)i(F_i)_i. (See for example Baireness of $C_k(X)$ for locally compact $X$ (Gruenhage & Ma).)

The equivalence between the two definitions is Theorem 5.1.17 of General Topology (Engelking, 1989).

Defined on page 168 of Counterexamples in Topology; also on page 305 of General Topology (Engelking, 1989) with the additional assumption of T1T_1, which we do not assume here.

Occasionally abbreviated as "CWN", as in Collectionwise Hausdorff versus collectionwise normal with respect to compact sets (Reed).

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is preserved by arbitrary disjoint unions.

P000090AlexandrovPredicate

An arbitrary intersection of open sets is open.

This is equivalent to each of the following:

  • An arbitrary union of closed sets is closed.
  • Each x∈Xx \in X has a smallest neighborhood.
  • For each x∈Xx \in X, the neighborhood kernel of xx, i. e. ⋂{U open in X∣x∈U}\bigcap\big\{U\text{ open in }X\mid x\in U\big\}, is open.
  • XX is finitely generated: For each A⊆XA \subseteq X, AA is open iff A∩YA \cap Y is open in the subspace YY for each finite Y⊆XY \subseteq X.
  • There is a preorder (i.e., a reflexive and transitive relation) ⪯\preceq on XX such that the open sets are precisely the upward closed sets (i.e., sets A⊆XA\subseteq X such that x∈Ax\in A and x⪯yx\preceq y imply y∈Ay\in A).

See Alexandrov Topology on Wikipedia for a more extensive list. See also Alexandroff spaces (F. G. Arenas).

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is hereditary.
  • This property is preserved by arbitrary disjoint unions.
  • This property is preserved by finite products.
  • This property is preserved by box products.

P000102SemimetrizablePredicate

For a set XX, a function d:X2→[0,∞)d:X^2\to[0,\infty) is called a symmetric if it satisfies reflexivity (d(x,y)=0⇔x=yd(x,y)=0\Leftrightarrow x=y) and symmetry (d(x,y)=d(y,x)d(x,y)=d(y,x)). A space XX is called semimetrizable if there is a symmetric d:X2→[0,∞)d:X^2\to[0,\infty) such that the balls Bd(x,ε)={y∈X:d(x,y)<ε}B_d(x,\varepsilon)=\{y\in X:d(x,y)<\varepsilon\} for ε>0\varepsilon>0 form a neighborhood basis at each point x∈Xx\in X. Such a symmetric is called a semimetric. (Note that A regular semi-metric space for which there is no semimetric under which all spheres are open (Heath) demonstrates that these neighborhood balls need not be open sets.)

Equivalently:

  • There exists a symmetric dd such that pp lies in the closure of some Y⊆XY\subseteq X iff d(p,Y)=inf⁡{d(p,y):y∈Y}=0d(p,Y)=\inf\{d(p,y):y\in Y\}=0. Such a symmetric is automatically a semimetric.
  • (i) XX is T1T_1; (ii) for each x∈Xx \in X, there is a non-increasing sequence of open sets {Gn(x):n<ω}\{G_n(x):n<\omega\} forming a local neighborhood basis for xx; (iii) if for some sequence xnx_n in XX, y∈Xy\in X belongs to Gn(xn)G_n(x_n) for all nn, then xn→yx_n\to y. This equivalence is shown in Theorem 3.2 of Arc-wise connectedness in semi-metric spaces (Heath).

Defined in e.g. Arc-wise connectedness in semi-metric spaces (Heath) and Generalized Metric Spaces and Mappings (Lin , Yun). Note that some sources, e.g., On semi-metric spaces (Wilson), use the term semimetric to refer to a symmetric and the term semimetrizable to refer to Symmetrizable.

P000109Monotonically normalPredicate

There are several equivalent definitions. See Monotonically normal space on Wikipedia for a few more.

Definition (1): (see Definition 2.1 in Monotonically normal spaces (Heath, Lutzer, Zenor))

The space is T1T_1 and there is a function GG that assigns to each ordered pair (A,B)(A,B) of disjoint closed sets in XX an open set G(A,B)G(A,B) such that:

  • (i) A⊆G(A,B)⊆G(A,B)‾⊆X∖BA\subseteq G(A,B)\subseteq \overline{G(A,B)}\subseteq X\setminus B;
  • (ii) G(A,B)⊆G(A′,B′)G(A,B)\subseteq G(A',B') whenever A⊆A′A\subseteq A' and B′⊆BB'\subseteq B.

The operator GG is called a monotone normality operator.

One can always choose GG to satisfy the property

G(A,B)∩G(B,A)=∅,\quad G(A,B)\cap G(B,A)=\emptyset,

by replacing each G(A,B)G(A,B) by G(A,B)∖G(B,A)‾G(A,B)\setminus\overline{G(B,A)}.

Definition (2): (see Theorem 2.2(e) in Mary Ellen Rudin and monotone normality (Bennett & Lutzer) and references there)

The space is T1T_1 and there is a function μ\mu that assigns to each pair (x,U)(x,U) with UU open in XX and x∈Ux\in U an open set μ(x,U)\mu(x,U) such that:

  • (i) x∈μ(x,U)x\in\mu(x,U);
  • (ii) if μ(x,U)∩μ(y,V)≠∅\mu(x,U)\cap\mu(y,V)\ne\emptyset, then x∈Vx\in V or y∈Uy\in U.

Such a function μ\mu automatically satisfies

x∈μ(x,U)⊆μ(x,U)‾⊆U\quad x\in\mu(x,U)\subseteq\overline{\mu(x,U)}\subseteq U.

Note 1: It is sufficient to assume the function μ\mu is defined for UU belonging to a base for the topology.

Note 2: It is not necessarily the case that μ(x,U)\mu(x,U) satisfies monotonicity in UU, that is, μ(x,U)⊆μ(x,U′)\mu(x,U)\subseteq\mu(x,U') if x∈U⊆U′x\in U\subseteq U'. But one can construct a modified function

ν(x,U)=⋃{μ(x,W):W open, x∈W⊆U}\quad \nu(x,U)=\bigcup\{\mu(x,W):W\text{ open, }x\in W\subseteq U\},

which does satisfy (i), (ii), and monotonicity in UU.

Equivalence between the two definitions: (see A study of monotonically normal spaces (Borges))

Given GG from Definition (1) with the condition G(A,B)∩G(B,A)=∅G(A,B)\cap G(B,A)=\emptyset, the function μ(x,U)=G({x},X∖U)\mu(x,U)=G(\{x\},X\setminus U) satisfies Definition (2).

Given μ\mu from Definition (2) and the associated function ν\nu, the function G(A,B)=⋃{ν(x,X∖B):x∈A}G(A,B)=\bigcup\{\nu(x,X\setminus B):x\in A\} satisfies Definition (1).

Meta-properties

  • This property is hereditary (easy consequence of Definition (2)).

P000110DevelopablePredicate

The space has a development.

A development for a space XX is a sequence 𝒰1,𝒰2,…\mathscr U_1,\mathscr U_2,\dots of open covers of XX such that for each x∈Xx\in X the collection {st⁡(x,𝒰n):n=1,2,… }\{\operatorname{st}(x,\mathscr U_n):n=1,2,\dots\} is a local base at xx. Here, st⁡(x,𝒰n)=⋃{U∈𝒰n:x∈U}\operatorname{st}(x,\mathscr U_n)=\bigcup\{U\in\mathscr U_n:x\in U\} is the star of xx with respect to 𝒰n\mathscr U_n.

Note: If XX has a development, one can always choose a development such that each 𝒰n+1\mathscr U_{n+1} is a refinement of 𝒰n\mathscr U_n.

P000115SubparacompactPredicate

Every open cover of XX has a σ\sigma-discrete closed refinement.

This is equivalent to each of the following:

  • Every open cover of XX has a σ\sigma-locally finite closed refinement.

  • Every open cover of XX has a σ\sigma-closure preserving closed refinement.

  • For every open cover 𝒰\mathscr U of XX, there is a sequence <𝒱n:n∈ω>\left<\mathscr V_n : n \in \omega\right> of open covers where each 𝒱n\mathscr V_n is a refinement of 𝒰\mathscr U and, for each x∈Xx \in X, there is some nn with st⁡(x,𝒱n)⊆U\operatorname{st}(x,\mathscr V_n)\subseteq U for some U∈𝒰U\in\mathscr U.

  • For every open cover 𝒰\mathscr U of XX, there is a sequence <𝒱n:n∈ω>\left<\mathscr V_n : n \in \omega\right> of open covers where each 𝒱n\mathscr V_n is a refinement of 𝒰\mathscr U and, for each x∈Xx \in X, there is some nn with ord⁡(x,𝒱n)=1\operatorname{ord}(x,\mathscr V_n)=1.

Some of the terms used above: For some topological property 𝒫\mathcal P, a collection of sets is called σ\sigma-𝒫\mathcal P if it is a countable union of collections, each satisfying 𝒫\mathcal P. For 𝒲\mathscr W a collection of subsets of XX, 𝒲\mathscr W is closure preserving if for each 𝒲′⊆𝒲\mathscr W'\subseteq\mathscr W, ⋃𝒲′‾=⋃{U‾:U∈𝒲′}\overline{\bigcup\mathscr W'}=\bigcup\{\overline U:U\in\mathscr W'\}. Also, st⁡(x,𝒲)=⋃{W∈𝒲:x∈W}\operatorname{st}(x,\mathscr W)=\bigcup\{W\in\mathscr W:x\in W\} and ord⁡(x,𝒲)=∣{W∈𝒲:x∈W}∣\operatorname{ord}(x,\mathscr W)=|\{W\in\mathscr W:x\in W\}|.

See Theorem 3.1 in Covering properties (D. Burke), Ch. 9 of Handbook of set-theoretic topology (the whole chapter assumes T2T_2, but that property is not used to show the equivalences) and Theorem V.7 on p. 217 in Modern General Topology (Nagata, 1985). See also Covering properties (D. Burke), Ch. 9 of Handbook of set-theoretic topology for references and original names for the properties when they were first introduced.

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is hereditary with respect to closed sets.

Sources cited by Pi-Base

  • Covering properties (D. Burke), Ch. 9 of Handbook of set-theoretic topology
  • Modern General Topology (Nagata, 1985)

P000117Has a σ\sigma-locally finite networkPredicate

A space with a σ\sigma-locally finite network.

A family 𝒩\mathcal N of subsets of XX is called a network if every open set is the union of a subfamily of 𝒩\mathcal N; that is, for every open set UU and point x∈Ux\in U there is some A∈𝒩A\in\mathcal N with x∈A⊆Ux\in A\subseteq U. The family 𝒩\mathcal N is σ\sigma-locally finite if it is a countable union of locally finite families.

See for example page 127 of General Topology (Engelking, 1989).

P000118Has a σ\sigma-locally finite kk-networkPredicate

The family 𝒩\mathcal N is σ\sigma-locally finite if it is a countable union of locally finite families.

P000120Locally orderablePredicate

Each point has a neighbourhood that is orderable (LOTS).

This is equivalent to each of the following:

  • Each point has an open neighbourhood that is orderable.
  • Each point has a local base of orderable neighbourhoods.
  • The topology of XX has a base consisting of orderable open sets.

The equivalences can be shown similarly to the proof of Proposition 2.4 in Locally ordered topological spaces (P. Pikul).

First introduced in the PhD dissertation of H. Herrlich Ordnungsfähigkeit topologischer Räume (Herrlich).

P000121PseudometrizablePredicate

A space XX whose topology is induced by some pseudometric.

A pseudometric on XX is a map d:X×X→ℝd:X\times X\to\Bbb{R} such that for all x,y,z∈Xx,y,z \in X (i) d(x,y)≥0d(x,y) \geq 0 and d(x,x)=0d(x,x)=0, (ii) d(x,y)=d(y,x)d(x,y) = d(y,x), (iii) d(x,z)≤d(x,y)+d(y,z)d(x,z) \leq d(x,y) + d(y,z). That is, a pseudometric satisfies the same properties as a metric, except that distinct points can have d(x,y)=0d(x,y)=0. The topology induced by dd is the topology generated by all the open balls B(x,ϵ)={y∈X:d(x,y)<ϵ}B(x,\epsilon) = \{y \in X:d(x,y)<\epsilon\} with x∈Xx\in X, ϵ>0\epsilon>0.

Defined in Example 3.2(a) of General Topology (Willard).

P000122Locally EuclideanPredicate

Each point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of ℝn\mathbb R^n with its Euclidean topology for some integer n≥0n\ge 0. Equivalently, each point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to ℝn\mathbb R^n for some nn. Note that the value of nn is allowed to differ between points; if it does not vary, then the space has the stronger property Locally nn-Euclidean.

In the case n=0n=0, a point with a neighborhood homeomorphic to ℝ0={0}\mathbb R^0=\{0\} is an isolated point.

Note: In all the above, one can equivalently require the neighborhoods to be open.

The closely related Locally nn-Euclidean property is defined on page 316 of Topology (Munkres) and on page 38 of Introduction to topological manifolds (Lee).

Meta-properties

  • This property is preserved by finite products.
  • This property is preserved by arbitrary disjoint unions.

P000134R1R_1Predicate

A space in which any two topologically distinguishable points can be separated by disjoint neighbourhoods. (Two points are topologically distinguishable if there is an open set containing one of the points and not the other.)

Equivalently, a space whose Kolmogorov quotient is Hausdorff.

Defined in Hausdorff space on Wikipedia, and in definition 16.10, p. 439 of Handbook of Analysis and its Foundations (Schechter).

Meta-properties

  • XX is R1R_1 iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) is T2T_2.
  • This property is hereditary.

P000135R0R_0Predicate

Given any two topologically distinguishable points, each has a neighborhood not including the other point. (Two points are topologically distinguishable if there is an open set containing one of the points and not the other.)

Equivalently, any of the following equivalent properties holds:

  • The Kolmogorov quotient of the space is T1T_1.
  • Every neighborhood of a point x∈Xx\in X contains cl⁡{x}\operatorname{cl}\{x\}.
  • Every open set is a union of closed sets.
  • For each x∈Xx\in X, the closure cl⁡{x}\operatorname{cl}\{x\} is precisely the set of points topologically indistinguishable from xx.
  • The closures of any two points are either identical or disjoint (so {cl⁡{x}∣x∈X}\{\operatorname{cl}\{x\}\mid x\in X\} is a partition of the space XX).

See T1 space on Wikipedia for a more extensive list.

Also defined in definition 16.6, p. 438 of Handbook of Analysis and its Foundations (Schechter) as "symmetric space". Not to be confused with symmetric spaces from Riemannian geometry.

Meta-properties

  • XX is R0R_0 iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) is T1T_1.
  • This property is preserved by arbitrary products and box products.
  • This property is hereditary.

Sources cited by Pi-Base

  • T1 space on Wikipedia
  • Handbook of Analysis and its Foundations (Schechter)

P000140k1k_1-spacePredicate

A space whose topology coincides with the final topology with respect to the family of all inclusions from compact subspaces. A subset A⊆XA\subseteq X is open (resp. closed) whenever A∩KA\cap K is open (resp. closed) in KK for every compact subspace KK of XX.

Equivalently, a space whose topology coincides with the final topology with respect to the family of all continuous maps from arbitrary compact spaces. A subset A⊆XA\subseteq X is open (resp. closed) whenever f−1(A)f^{-1}(A) is open (resp. closed) in KK for every compact space KK and every continuous map f:K→Xf:K\to X.

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is hereditary with respect to closed sets.
  • This property is not hereditary with respect to open sets (e.g., Arens-Fort Space, open in One-point compactification of the Arens-Fort space).

P000145Strongly paracompactPredicate

Every open cover has a star-finite open refinement.

A family 𝒜\mathscr A of subsets of XX is called star-finite if each element of 𝒜\mathscr A meets at most finitely many elements of 𝒜\mathscr A.

Defined on p. 326 of General Topology (Engelking, 1989) together with the condition that the space is T2T_2. Here we do not assume any separation axiom as part of the definition. Also called hypocompact, for example in Definition 2 of On some generalized compactness properties (J. Greever).

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is preserved by arbitrary disjoint unions.

P000146UltraparacompactPredicate

Every open cover 𝒰\mathscr U of XX has an open (hence clopen) refinement 𝒱\mathscr V partitioning XX. (We do not assume T2T_2.)

(Note: One can always choose the same index set for the two covers. Given 𝒰={Ui:i∈I}\mathscr U=\{U_i:i\in I\}, one can choose 𝒱={Vi:i∈I}\mathscr V=\{V_i:i\in I\} with Vi⊆UiV_i\subseteq U_i for each ii.)

Equivalently, every open cover of the space is refined by a locally finite clopen cover.

The equivalence between the two definitions is shown in Lemma 1.3 and Corollary 1.4 of Extending continuous functions on zero-dimensional spaces (R. Ellis).

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is preserved by arbitrary disjoint unions.

Sources cited by Pi-Base

  • Ultraparacompactness and Ultranormality (J. Van Name)
  • Extending continuous functions on zero-dimensional spaces (R. Ellis)

P000147P-spacePredicate

A space in which every countable intersection of open sets is open.

Equivalently, a space in which every countable union of closed sets is closed.

Equivalently, a space in which every point is a P-point, that is, a point for which the family of neighborhoods is closed under countable intersections.

Defined in A topological view of P-spaces (A. Misra) with the additional assumption of T1T_1, which is not assumed here.

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.

P000149ω\omega-LindelöfPredicate

Every ω\omega-cover of XX has a countable ω\omega-subcover. (A family 𝒰\mathcal U of open subsets of XX is called an ω\omega-cover if each finite subset of XX is contained in an element of 𝒰\mathcal U and X∉𝒰X \notin \mathcal U.)

Equivalently, every finite power of XX is Lindelöf.

See Some properties of C(X), I (Gerlits & Nagy); the equivalence with every finite power being Lindelöf is on page 156.

The name ω\omega-Lindelöf used in e.g. Selection principles related to α-properties (Kočinac) is motivated as the adaptation of Lindelöf for ω\omega-covers. This property is often called ε\varepsilon-space as it originally appeared as the fifth item "ε\varepsilon" in a list from Some properties of C(X), I (Gerlits & Nagy).

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is hereditary with respect to closed sets.

P000151Strategically RothbergerPredicate

Strategically Rothberger: The second player has a winning strategy in the Rothberger game 𝖦1(𝒪X,𝒪X)\mathsf{G}_1(\mathcal O_X,\mathcal O_X). See pages 2 and 3 of Limited information strategies and discrete selectivity (Clontz & Holshouser) for more details.

Strategically Ω\Omega-Rothberger: The second player has a winning strategy in the game 𝖦1(ΩX,ΩX)\mathsf{G}_1(\Omega_X,\Omega_X). See pages 2 and 3 of Limited information strategies and discrete selectivity (Clontz & Holshouser) for more details.

Theorem 15 of Limited information strategies and discrete selectivity (Clontz & Holshouser) states the equivalence for T312T_{3 \frac{1}{2}} spaces, but the equivalence is shown to not require any separation axiom at Can P1 improve an open cover to an omega-cover in the finite-open game?.

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • XX satisfies the property if it is a countable union of subspaces with the property (idea: interleave strategies, one for each subspace).

Sources cited by Pi-Base

  • Limited information strategies and discrete selectivity (Clontz & Holshouser)
  • Can P1 improve an open cover to an omega-cover in the finite-open game?

P000152Markov RothbergerPredicate

The second player has a Markov winning strategy in the Rothberger game 𝖦1(𝒪X,𝒪X)\mathsf{G}_1(\mathcal O_X,\mathcal O_X) (relying on only the round number and most recent move of the opponent). See pages 2 and 3 of Limited information strategies and discrete selectivity (Clontz & Holshouser) for more details.

Equivalent conditions:

  • Markov Ω\Omega-Rothberger: The second player has a Markov winning strategy in the game 𝖦1(ΩX,ΩX)\mathsf{G}_1(\Omega_X,\Omega_X) (relying on only the round number and most recent move of the opponent). See pages 2 and 3 of Limited information strategies and discrete selectivity (Clontz & Holshouser) for more details.

  • Topologically countable: There is a set {xn:n∈ω}⊆X\{ x_n : n \in \omega \} \subseteq X so that, for every x∈Xx \in X, there is some n∈ωn \in \omega so that every neighborhood of xnx_n contains xx. See On traditional Menger and Rothberger variations (Caruvana, Clontz, Holshouser) for more on this property.

The equivalence is shown in Theorem 4.17 of On traditional Menger and Rothberger variations (Caruvana, Clontz, Holshouser) and also at Do uncountable spaces admit Markov strategies in Rothberger-style games?.

P000154GO-spacePredicate

The space XX is T1T_1 and there is a linear order << on XX such that every point has a local base of order-convex neighborhoods. (A subset AA of an ordered set (X,<)(X,<) is order-convex if for each a,b∈Aa,b\in A with a<ba<b, AA contains all points of XX between aa and bb.)

Equivalently, there is a linear order << on XX such that rays (a,→)={x:a<x}(a,\rightarrow)=\{x:a<x\} and (←,b)={x:x<b}(\leftarrow,b)=\{x:x<b\} are open, and every point has a local base of order-convex neighborhoods.

Equivalently, XX is homeomorphic to a subspace of a LOTS.

Equivalently, XX is homeomorphic to a closed subspace of a LOTS.

For more details and the proof of these equivalences, see On generalized ordered spaces (D. Lutzer) (https://eudml.org/doc/268514) and Equivalent definitions for GO-spaces (generalized ordered spaces).

Such spaces are also called suborderable (as an example, in The existence of continuous weak selections and orderability-type properties in products and filter spaces (Motooka et al.)).

Meta-properties

  • This property is hereditary.

Sources cited by Pi-Base

  • On generalized ordered spaces (D. Lutzer)
  • Equivalent definitions for GO-spaces (generalized ordered spaces)
  • The existence of continuous weak selections and orderability-type properties in products and filter spaces (Motooka et al.)

P000162RealcompactPredicate

A space XX that is homeomorphic to a closed subset of ℝκ\mathbb{R}^\kappa for some cardinal κ\kappa.

Equivalently (see Rings of Continuous Functions (Gillman and Jerison)), XX is T312T_{3 \frac{1}{2}} and every real zz-ultrafilter 𝒰\mathcal U on the space XX is fixed, that is, ⋂𝒰≠∅\bigcap\mathcal{U}\neq\emptyset.

A zz-ultrafilter is an ultrafilter on the lattice of zero-sets of XX (see Ultrafilter on Wikipedia for the general definition of an ultrafilter on a poset). A real zz-ultrafilter is a zz-ultrafilter with countable intersection property, that is, for any countable ℱ⊆𝒰\mathcal{F}\subseteq \mathcal{U} we have ⋂ℱ≠∅\bigcap\mathcal{F}\neq \emptyset.

See also section 3.11 in General Topology (Engelking, 1989).

Note: If XX has Cardinality less than every measurable cardinal, then XX is Dieudonné complete iff Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) is Realcompact.

Sources cited by Pi-Base

  • General Topology (Engelking, 1989)
  • Rings of Continuous Functions (Gillman and Jerison)

P000164Cardinality less than every measurable cardinalPredicate

The cardinality of the space is smaller than every measurable cardinal, if one exists.

A cardinal κ\kappa is called measurable if κ\kappa is uncountable and there exists a measure μ:2κ→{0,1}\mu:2^\kappa\to \{0, 1\} such that

  1. μ\mu is κ\kappa-additive: μ(⋃i∈IAi)=∑i∈Iμ(Ai)\mu(\bigcup_{i\in I} A_i) = \sum_{i\in I} \mu(A_i) for any family (Ai)i∈I⊆2κ(A_i)_{i\in I}\subseteq 2^\kappa of pairwise disjoint sets with ∣I∣<κ|I| < \kappa,

  2. μ\mu is non-trivial: μ(κ)=1\mu(\kappa) = 1 and μ({x})=0\mu(\{x\}) = 0 for all x∈κx\in \kappa.

Equivalently, κ\kappa is uncountable and there exists a free ultrafilter 𝒰\mathcal{U} on κ\kappa such that 𝒰\mathcal{U} is κ\kappa-complete, i.e., if ℱ⊆𝒰\mathcal{F}\subseteq \mathcal{U} and ∣ℱ∣<κ|\mathcal{F}| < \kappa then ⋂ℱ∈𝒰\bigcap\mathcal{F}\in \mathcal{U}. (See Measurable cardinal on Wikipedia for more details.)

Note: Some authors, for example Rings of Continuous Functions (Gillman and Jerison), refer to measurable cardinals as those cardinals κ\kappa for which there exists a σ\sigma-additive measure μ:2κ→{0,1}\mu:2^\kappa\to \{0, 1\} which is non-trivial. If κ\kappa is the smallest such cardinal, then a non-trivial σ\sigma-additive measure μ:2κ→{0,1}\mu:2^\kappa\to \{0, 1\} is κ\kappa-additive (see lemma 10.2 of Set Theory (Jech) and comments preceding it), so κ\kappa is also measurable by the above definition.

(The existence of a measurable cardinal cannot be proven in ZFC. So spaces whose construction does not depend on set-theoretic axioms beyond ZFC should never have this property marked as false.)

Meta-properties

  • This property is hereditary.

  • Rings of Continuous Functions (Gillman and Jerison)
  • Set Theory (Jech)

P000165PseudonormalPredicate

For every countable closed set HH and open set U⊇HU\supseteq H, there exists an open set VV with H⊆V⊆cl(V)⊆UH\subseteq V\subseteq cl(V)\subseteq U. In other words, countable closed sets have arbitrarily small closed neighborhoods.

Equivalently, any two disjoint closed sets, at least one of which is countable, can be separated by open sets.

Defined for example on p. 8 of Pseudocompact topological spaces (Hrusak et al.).

See also https://dantopology.wordpress.com/2014/02/17/pseudonormal-spaces/.

P000170k1k_1-HausdorffPredicate

P000174Well-basedPredicate

Each point x∈Xx\in X has a neighborhood base well-ordered by reverse inclusion.

Equivalently, each point x∈Xx\in X has a neighborhood base totally ordered by reverse inclusion. The two are equivalent since a linear order admits a well-ordered cofinal subset.

Such spaces are called well-based in An internal characterisation of radiality (R. Leek) and lob-spaces (lob = "linearly ordered (local) base") in mr 0540476.

One says that XX is well-based at the point xx if the conditions above hold at the specific point. So XX is well-based if it is well-based at every point.

See also Convergent filters generated by (not necessarily countable) chains and Name for topological spaces where 'every point has a local base wellordered by reverse inclusion'.

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is hereditary.

P000182Has a countable networkPredicate

A space with a (finite or infinite) countable network.

A family 𝒩\mathcal N of subsets of XX is called a network if every open set is the union of a subfamily of 𝒩\mathcal N. That is, for every open set UU and point x∈Ux\in U there is some A∈𝒩A\in\mathcal N with x∈A⊆Ux\in A\subseteq U.

P000183Has a countable kk-networkPredicate

A space with a (finite or infinite) countable kk-network.

Equivalently:

  • A space with countable pseudobase.
  • A space with countable cscs-network.
  • A space with countable cs∗cs^\ast-network.

A family 𝒩\mathcal N of subsets of XX is called a kk-network if for every compact set KK and open set UU in XX with K⊆UK\subseteq U, there exists a finite 𝒩∗⊆𝒩\mathcal{N}^* \subseteq \mathcal{N} with K⊆⋃𝒩∗⊆UK \subseteq \bigcup\mathcal{N}^* \subseteq U.

A family 𝒩\mathcal{N} of subsets of XX is called a pseudobase if for every compact set KK and open set UU in XX with K⊆UK\subseteq U, there exists some A∈𝒩A\in\mathcal{N} with K⊆A⊆UK \subseteq A \subseteq U.

A family 𝒩\mathcal{N} of subsets of XX is called a cscs-network if for every open set U⊆XU\subseteq X, point x∈Ux\in U and sequence (xn)(x_n) converging to xx, there exists some A∈𝒩A\in\mathcal{N} with xn∈Ax_n\in A for all but finitely many nn.

A family 𝒩\mathcal{N} of subsets of XX is called a cs∗cs^\ast-network if for every open set U⊆XU\subseteq X, point x∈Ux\in U and sequence (xn)(x_n) converging to xx, there exists some A∈𝒩A\in\mathcal{N} with xn∈Ax_n\in A for infinitely many nn.

To see the equivalence, first note that a pseudobase is a kk-network, a kk-network is a cscs-network and a cscs-network is a cs∗cs^\ast-network. In Answer to "Product of spaces with countable $k$-networks" it is shown that if XX has countable cs∗cs^\ast-network, then it has a countable kk-network. Then finite unions of elements of that kk-network form a countable pseudobase.

See $\aleph_0$-spaces (E. Michael), available at https://www.jstor.org/stable/24901448.

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is hereditary.
  • This property is preserved by countable products (see Corollary in Answer to "Product of spaces with countable $k$-networks").

Sources cited by Pi-Base

  • $\aleph_0$-spaces (E. Michael)
  • $\mathfrak P$-spaces and related concepts (Gabriyelyan & Kakol)
  • Answer to "Product of spaces with countable $k$-networks"

P000187W-spacePredicate

P1 has a winning strategy at each point x∈Xx\in X for the following game defined by Gruenhage in Infinite games and generalizations of first-countable spaces (Gruenhage).

During each round n<ωn<\omega, P1 chooses some neighborhood UnU_n of xx, then P2 chooses some point xn∈Unx_n\in U_n. P1 wins provided the sequence of xnx_n converges to xx; P2 wins otherwise.

See also section 2 of The story of a topological game (Gruenhage).

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is hereditary.
  • This property is preserved by countable products (see Theorem 4.1 of Infinite games and generalizations of first-countable spaces (Gruenhage)).
  • This property is preserved by Σ\Sigma-products (see Theorem 4.6 of Infinite games and generalizations of first-countable spaces (Gruenhage)).
  • A locally WW-space (every point has a neighborhood with the property) is a WW-space.

P000189σ\sigma-connectedPredicate

The space cannot be partitioned into more than one and at most countably infinitely many nonempty closed sets.

Equivalently, XX is Connected and cannot be written as a countably infinite union of pairwise disjoint nonempty closed sets.

Equivalently, every continuous map from XX to Cofinite topology on ω\omega is constant. (This is easy to check using the fact that the codomain is countable and T1T_1, and each of its proper closed subsets is a finite union of singletons.)

Defined in Chapter 5, Section 4, Definition 5.15 of Continuum Theory: An introduction (Nadler).

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • If a dense subspace of XX satisfies this property, so does XX (see Fact 3 in Answer to "$\sigma$-connected spaces and path-connected property").
  • The continuous image of a σ\sigma-connected space is σ\sigma-connected (see Fact 2 in Answer to "$\sigma$-connected spaces and path-connected property").

P000194SubmetacompactPredicate

P000195Stone spacePredicate

The space is Compact, T2T_2, and Totally disconnected.

This is equivalent to each of the following:

  • The space is Compact and Totally separated.
  • The space is Compact, T0T_0, and Zero dimensional.
  • The space is Spectral and T1T_1.

The equivalence follows from various theorems in pi-base.

Also known as profinite spaces, referring to the fact that such spaces are precisely the cofiltered limits of finite discrete spaces. See the section on Profinite spaces at the Stacks project.

Not to be confused with Stonean, which is a stronger property.

P000200Simply connectedPredicate

Every pair of points in XX is connected by a unique homotopy class of paths. (See Proposition 1.6. of Algebraic Topology (Hatcher).)

This is equivalent to each of the following:

  • XX is Path connected and every continuous map S1→XS^1 \to X extends to a continuous map D2→XD^2 \to X.
  • XX is Path connected and every continuous map S1→XS^1 \to X is homotopic to a constant map.

In case X≠∅X\ne\emptyset, it is equivalent to the usual formulation:

  • XX is Path connected and the fundamental group π1(X)\pi_1(X) is trivial.

Note: The fundamental group is undefined for the empty space.

Also called 11-connected if X≠∅X\ne\emptyset. See n-connected space in nLab.

Defined on page 28 of Algebraic Topology (Hatcher). See Characterizing simply connected spaces for additional equivalent characterizations.

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is preserved by arbitrary products.

P000201Has a generic pointPredicate

There exists a generic point p∈Xp \in X.

The point pp is called a generic point of XX if any of the following equivalent conditions holds:

  • {p}\{p\} is dense in XX.
  • XX is the only closed set containing pp.
  • pp is an element of every nonempty open subset of XX.
  • pp is a generalization of every point of XX, according to the specialization preorder. See Specialization (pre)order on Wikipedia.
  • The topology is coarser than or equal to an included point/particular point topology (e.g. Particular point topology on a countably infinite set).

Compare with Has a point with a unique neighborhood.

See Definition 1.1.7 on page 3 of Algebraic Geometry II (Mumford-Oda).

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is preserved in any coarser topology.

P000202Has a point with a unique neighborhoodPredicate

P000203Almost discretePredicate

All points except for one are isolated.

Equivalently, the topology is not Discrete and is equal to or finer than an excluded point topology (e.g. Excluded Point Topology on a Countably Infinite Set).

There have been various slightly different definitions of "almost discrete" in the literature. Most definitions exclude discrete spaces; see for example Almost discrete SV-spaces (Henrikson, Wilson) and On the product of almost discrete Grothendieck spaces (Osipov). Sometimes T2T_2 is assumed, but we don't make that assumption here.

Compare with Has a point with a unique neighborhood.

P000206Strongly ChoquetPredicate

Player 2 has a winning strategy in the strong Choquet game played on a nonempty space.

Let V−1=XV_{-1}=X. During round n<ωn<\omega of this game, Player 1 chooses a point xnx_n with an open neighborhood Un⊆Vn−1U_n\subseteq V_{n-1}, and Player 2 chooses some open neighborhood Vn⊆UnV_n\subseteq U_n of xnx_n.

Player 2 wins this game provided ⋂{Un:n<ω}  (=⋂{Vn:n<ω})≠∅\bigcap\{U_n:n<\omega\}\; (= \bigcap\{V_n:n<\omega\}) \not=\emptyset.

Note: We consider the Empty space to be Strongly Choquet in the sense that Player 1 cannot make a legal move to start the game, and therefore loses immediately according to the Normal play convention on Wikipedia of combinatorial games.

P000207Strongly collectionwise normalPredicate

For each neighborhood UU of the diagonal Δ={(x,x)∣x∈X}\Delta=\{(x,x)\mid x\in X\} in X×XX\times X, there is a neighborhood VV of the diagonal such that V∘V⊆UV\circ V\subseteq U.

This is equivalent to the family 𝒰\mathcal{U} of neighborhoods of ΔX\Delta_X forming a uniformity, but the topology of XX and that of (X,𝒰)(X, \mathcal{U}) do not need to agree. If XX is Completely regular then both topologies coincide.

In Theorem 2.6 of doi 10.2307/1993026 this property was shown to be equivalent to almost 22-fully normal: each open cover 𝒰\mathcal U has an open almost 22-star refinement 𝒱\mathcal V, that is 𝒱\mathcal{V} is a refinement of 𝒰\mathcal{U} and for any x,y,zx, y, z with y,z∈St(x,𝒱)y, z\in \text{St}(x, \mathcal{V}) there exists U∈𝒰U\in\mathcal{U} with y,z∈Uy, z\in U.

Originally studied by Cohen in Sur une problème de M. Dieudonné (Cohen) (http://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k3186w/f290.image), where it was shown to be strictly stronger than Collectionwise normal. See also Strong collectionwise normality and M. E. Rudin’s Dowker space (Hart).

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is preserved by arbitrary disjoint unions.
  • This property is hereditary with respect to closed sets (corollary of Theorem 4.1 in Some generalizations of full normality (M. J. Mansfield)).

P000208NoetherianPredicate

Every subset of XX is compact.

Equivalently:

  • Every open set is compact.
  • The open sets satisfy the ascending chain condition: There is no infinite strictly increasing sequence O1⊊O2⊊⋯O_1 \subsetneq O_2 \subsetneq \cdots of open sets.
  • The closed sets satisfy the descending chain condition: There is no infinite strictly decreasing sequence Y1⊋Y2⊋⋯Y_1 \supsetneq Y_2 \supsetneq \cdots of closed sets.
  • Every nonempty collection of open sets has a maximal element.
  • Every nonempty collection of closed sets has a minimal element.

Defined on page 5 of Algebraic Geometry II (Mumford-Oda), and on page 248 of Spectral spaces (Dickmann, Schwartz, Tressl). Also see the section on Noetherian topological spaces from the Stacks project.

Compare with Artinian.

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is hereditary.
  • This property is preserved by finite products (see Theorem 3 in Answer to "Is the product of two Artinian topological spaces Artinian?").
  • This property is preserved by finite disjoint unions.
  • This property is preserved in any coarser topology.

P000210α1\alpha_1Predicate

For every x∈Xx\in X and every sequence of countably infinite sets S1,S2,⋯⊆XS_1,S_2,\dots\subseteq X with each SnS_n converging to xx, there is a countably infinite set S⊆⋃nSnS\subseteq\bigcup_n S_n such that SS converges to xx and S∩SnS\cap S_n is cofinite in SnS_n (i.e., Sn∖SS_n\setminus S is finite) for all nn.

Equivalently, the same condition holds with the additional requirement that the sets SnS_n are pairwise disjoint. (The equivalence is shown after Definition 1.1 in Arhangel'skii sheaf amalgamations in topological groups (Tsaban & Zdomskyy).)

Terminology: A countably infinite set A⊆XA\subseteq X converges to xx if some (equivalently, all) bijective enumeration of AA converges to xx; that is, if every neighborhood of xx contains all but finitely many elements of AA.

The definition above in terms of countably infinite sets follows Arhangel'skii sheaf amalgamations in topological groups (Tsaban & Zdomskyy). One can also phrase the definition in terms of (injective) sequences of elements of XX, as done in Subsets of ${}^\omega\omega$ and the Fréchet-Urysohn and $\alpha_i$-properties (P. Nyikos).

The αi\alpha_i properties for i=1,2,3,4i = 1, 2, 3, 4 (sometimes called "sheaf amalgamation properties") are due to Arkhangel'skii (The frequency spectrum of a topological space and the classification of spaces (A. V. Arkhangel'skii)).

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does (see Does the Arkhangel'skii $\alpha_1$ property hold for $X$ if it holds for its Kolmogorov quotient?).
  • This property is hereditary.
  • This property is preserved by countable products (see Answer to "Are the Arkhangel'skii $\alpha_i$ properties preserved by finite products?").
  • This property is preserved by arbitrary disjoint unions.
  • XX satisfies this property iff all its countable subspaces do.

Equivalently, the same condition holds with the additional requirement that the sets SnS_n are pairwise disjoint. (The equivalence follows from Lemma 1.2 in Subsets of ${}^\omega\omega$ and the Fréchet-Urysohn and $\alpha_i$-properties (P. Nyikos).)

Terminology: A countably infinite set A⊆XA\subseteq X converges to xx if some (equivalently, all) bijective enumeration of AA converges to xx; that is, if every neighborhood of xx contains all but finitely many elements of AA.

The definition above in terms of countably infinite sets follows Arhangel'skii sheaf amalgamations in topological groups (Tsaban & Zdomskyy). One can also phrase the definition in terms of (injective) sequences of elements of XX, as done in Subsets of ${}^\omega\omega$ and the Fréchet-Urysohn and $\alpha_i$-properties (P. Nyikos).

The αi\alpha_i properties for i=1,2,3,4i = 1, 2, 3, 4 (sometimes called "sheaf amalgamation properties") are due to Arkhangel'skii (The frequency spectrum of a topological space and the classification of spaces (A. V. Arkhangel'skii)).

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does (see Does the Arkhangel'skii $\alpha_1$ property hold for $X$ if it holds for its Kolmogorov quotient?).
  • This property is hereditary.
  • This property is preserved by countable products (see Answer to "Are the Arkhangel'skii $\alpha_i$ properties preserved by finite products?").
  • This property is preserved by arbitrary disjoint unions.
  • XX satisfies this property iff all its countable subspaces do.

P000217Strongly zero-dimensionalPredicate

Any two disjoint zero-sets are contained in disjoint clopen sets.

(Note: The clopen sets can always be chosen to be complement of each other.)

Equivalently:

  • Every finite cozero cover of XX has a finite clopen refinement which is a partition of XX (see definition p. 360 and Theorem 6.2.4 in General Topology (Engelking, 1989)).

If XX is T312T_{3 \frac{1}{2}}, this is also equivalent to:

  • The Stone–Čech compactification βX\beta X is Zero dimensional (see Theorems 16.11 and 16.17 in Rings of Continuous Functions (Gillman & Jerison)).

Some terminology used above: A zero-set is a set of the form f−1(0)f^{-1}(0) for some continuous f:X→ℝf:X\to\mathbb{R}. A cozero set is the complement of a zero-set.

Defined in section 6.2 of General Topology (Engelking, 1989) with the additional conditions that XX be Tychonoff (T312T_{3 \frac{1}{2}}) and non-empty. Here we do not require these two conditions.

See also page 4 of Ultraparacompactness and Ultranormality (J. Van Name).

The book Dimension theory (M. Charalambous) uses "strongly zero-dimensional" with the meaning of non-empty Ultranormal. The property Strongly zero-dimensional is equivalent to dim⁡0(X)≤0\dim_0(X) \leq 0 where dim⁡0\dim_0 is defined in chapter 11.

Meta-properties

P000221Dieudonné completePredicate

There exists at least one complete uniformity that induces the topology of XX.

This is equivalent to each of the following:

  • XX is homeomorphic to a closed subspace of a product of completely pseudometrizable spaces.
  • XX is homeomorphic to a closed subspace of a product of Pseudometrizable spaces.

For the equivalence, see Problem 8.5.13(z) in General Topology (Engelking, 1989) and page 285 of Sur les espaces uniformes complets (Dieudonné).

Terminology: We call a uniformity 𝒰\mathcal{U} complete if every Cauchy filter ℱ\mathcal{F} on (X,𝒰)(X, \mathcal{U}) converges. Equivalently, every Cauchy net (xi)i∈I(x_i)_{i\in I} on (X,𝒰)(X, \mathcal{U}) converges. Here a Cauchy filter is a filter ℱ\mathcal{F} such that for every U∈𝒰U\in\mathcal{U} there exists A∈ℱA\in\mathcal{F} such that A×A⊆UA\times A\subseteq U. A Cauchy net is a net (xi)i∈I(x_i)_{i\in I} such that for every U∈𝒰U\in\mathcal{U} there exists i0i_0 such that (xj,xk)∈U(x_j, x_k)\in U for j,k≥i0j, k\geq i_0. (Compare with the definition of complete uniformity in 15.7 of Rings of Continuous Functions (Gillman & Jerison) where uniform structure is defined using pseudometrics.)

Such spaces are called Dieudonné complete (Problem 8.5.13 in General Topology (Engelking, 1989)) or completely uniformizable (Problem 39B in General Topology (Willard, 1970)). They are called topologically complete on page 208 of General Topology (Kelley); this last term has also been used for Completely metrizable and Čech complete.

Note: If XX has Cardinality less than every measurable cardinal, then XX is Dieudonné complete iff Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) is Realcompact.

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is preserved by arbitrary products.
  • This property is hereditary with respect to closed sets.

P000225LCLCPredicate

XX is locally contractible at the point xx for all x∈Xx \in X, in the sense that every neighborhood UU of xx contains a neighborhood (equivalently, an open neighborhood) VV of xx that is contractible in UU; i.e., such that the inclusion map V↪UV \hookrightarrow U is null-homotopic.

Equivalently, every neighborhood UU of any point xx contains a neighborhood (or an open neighborhood) VV of xx such that the inclusion map V↪UV \hookrightarrow U is homotopic to the constant map with value xx.

This is the standard definition of "locally contractible" in the theory of ANRs, as originally introduced by Borsuk. Defined as locally contractible on page 28 of Theory of retracts (Borsuk), page 347 of Geometric aspects of general topology. (Sakai), and page 341 of Encyclopedia of general topology. The abbreviation LCLC is commonly used in this context.

P000226ArtinianPredicate

Every nonempty collection of open sets has a minimal element.

Equivalently:

  • Every nonempty collection of closed sets has a maximal element.
  • The open sets satisfy the descending chain condition: There is no infinite strictly decreasing sequence O1⊋O2⊋⋯O_1 \supsetneq O_2 \supsetneq \cdots of open sets.
  • The closed sets satisfy the ascending chain condition: There is no infinite strictly increasing sequence Y1⊊Y2⊊⋯Y_1 \subsetneq Y_2 \subsetneq \cdots of closed sets.
  • Every subspace has a finite dense subset.

See Equivalent definitions of an Artinian space for a proof of the equivalences.

Compare with Noetherian.

Meta-properties

  • This property is hereditary.
  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is preserved by finite disjoint unions.
  • This property is preserved by finite products (see Is the product of two Artinian topological spaces Artinian?).

P000232LC1LC^1Predicate

XX is locally 00-connected and locally 11-connected.

Following Borsuk's terminology (see page 30 of Theory of retracts (Borsuk)), this is the case n=1n=1 in the hierarchy of LCnLC^n properties. A space XX is locally nn-connected if for each x∈Xx\in X every neighborhood NN of xx contains a neighborhood UU of xx such that every map Sn→NS^n \to N with values in UU is null-homotopic in NN. And XX satisfies the LCnLC^n property if it is locally kk-connected for k=0,1,…,nk=0,1,\dots,n. (Note: LC0LC^0 is equivalent to Locally path connected.)

Equivalently, for each x∈Xx \in X, every neighborhood NN of xx contains a Path connected neighborhood UU of xx such that every loop ϕ:S1→U\phi:S^1\to U is null-homotopic in NN. See Is Borsuk's definition of $LC^1$ equivalent to this formulation of 'locally simply connected' ($P_{10}$)?.

Some authors, for example Lectures on algebraic topology (Dold) and Geometric aspects of general topology. (Sakai), use "locally 1-connected" with the meaning of LC1LC^1. Has also been called "locally simply connected", for example in Acyclicity in three-manifolds (McMillan). Listed as property P10P_{10} in Definition of locally simply connected space.

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is preserved by retractions (use Theorem 16.2 on p. 29 of Theory of retracts (Borsuk)).

P000233Has open path componentsPredicate

Every path component of XX is open.

This is equivalent to each of the following:

  • Each point x∈Xx\in X has a path connected neighborhood.

  • Each point x∈Xx\in X has an open path connected neighborhood.

  • XX is a topological disjoint union of Path connected spaces.

The equivalence between the various conditions can be shown by arguments similar to those used in the definition of Locally path connected, in particular Answer to "Definition of locally pathwise connected".

This property is used in the literature, but usually without a separate name. One exception is Topologies determined by paths (S. Franklin, B. Smith-Thomas) (accessible here), where it is called "PCGS" (path connectedly generated space).

Compare with Locally path connected and Has open connected components.

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is hereditary with respect to clopen sets.
  • This property is preserved by finite products.
  • This property is preserved by arbitrary disjoint unions.

Sources cited by Pi-Base

  • Topologies determined by paths (S. Franklin, B. Smith-Thomas)
  • Answer to "Definition of locally pathwise connected"

P000234Has open connected componentsPredicate

Every connected component of XX is open.

This is equivalent to each of the following:

  • Each point x∈Xx\in X has a connected neighborhood.

  • Each point x∈Xx\in X has an open connected neighborhood.

  • XX is a topological disjoint union of Connected spaces.

The equivalence between the various conditions can be shown by arguments similar to those used in the definition of Locally path connected, in particular Answer to "Definition of locally pathwise connected".

This property is normally used without a separate name. But see Topologies determined by paths (S. Franklin, B. Smith-Thomas) (accessible here), where it is called "CGS" (connectedly generated space).

Compare with Locally connected and Has open path components.

P000235Locally a Euclidean half-spacePredicate

Each point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of the closed upper half-space ℝ+n\mathbb R^n_+ for some integer n≥0n\ge 0, where

ℝ+n:={(x1,…,xn)∈ℝn:xn≥0}\quad\quad\mathbb R^n_+:=\{(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in\mathbb R^n : x_n\ge 0\}

has the Euclidean subspace topology. Equivalently, each point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to ℝ+n\mathbb R^n_+ for some nn. Note that the value of nn is allowed to differ between points; if it does not vary, then the space has the stronger property Locally an nn-Euclidean half-space.

In the case n=0n=0, the half-space ℝ+0\mathbb R^0_+ is considered the same as ℝ0={0}\mathbb R^0=\{0\}; thus a point with a neighborhood homeomorphic to ℝ+0\mathbb R^0_+ is an isolated point.

An equivalent condition for non-isolated points p∈Xp\in X is that one of the following holds:

  • ("manifold interior" point) pp has a neighborhood homeomorphic to ℝn;\mathbb R^n;
  • ("manifold boundary" point) pp has a neighborhood homeomorphic to ℝ+n\mathbb R^n_+ with pp mapped to a point of ∂ℝ+n:={x∈ℝn:xn=0}\partial\mathbb R^n_+:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n: x_n=0\}.

Note: In all the above, one can equivalently require the neighborhoods to be open.

The closely related Locally an nn-Euclidean half-space property is the main ingredient used to define Topological nn-manifold with boundary.

P000236Locally an nn-Euclidean half-spacePredicate

There exists some integer n≥0n\ge 0 such that each point of XX has a neighborhood homeomorphic to an open subset of the closed upper half-space ℝ+n\mathbb R^n_+, where

ℝ+n:={(x1,…,xn)∈ℝn:xn≥0}\quad\quad\mathbb R^n_+:=\{(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in\mathbb R^n : x_n\ge 0\}

has the Euclidean subspace topology. Equivalently, each point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to ℝ+n\mathbb R^n_+. Note that the value of nn is not allowed to differ between points; if it can vary, then the space has the weaker property Locally a Euclidean half-space.

In the case n=0n=0, the half-space ℝ+0\mathbb R^0_+ is considered the same as ℝ0={0}\mathbb R^0=\{0\}; thus a point with a neighborhood homeomorphic to ℝ+0\mathbb R^0_+ is an isolated point.

Equivalently when n>0n>0, each point p∈Xp\in X satisfies one of the following:

  • ("manifold interior" point) pp has a neighborhood homeomorphic to ℝn;\mathbb R^n;
  • ("manifold boundary" point) pp has a neighborhood homeomorphic to ℝ+n\mathbb R^n_+ with pp mapped to a point of ∂ℝ+n:={x∈ℝn:xn=0}\partial\mathbb R^n_+:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n: x_n=0\}.

Note: In all the above, one can equivalently require the neighborhoods to be open.

This property is the main ingredient in the definition of Topological nn-manifold with boundary.

Mentioned on page 42 of Introduction to topological manifolds (Lee, 2011). See also Manifold with boundary on Wikipedia.

P000238Has a real TVS topologyPredicate

XX is homeomorphic to a topological vector space (TVS) over ℝ\mathbb R.

Equivalently, there exists a continuous commutative group operation (x,y)↦x+y(x, y) \mapsto x + y on XX, and a continuous scalar multiplication operation ℝ×X→X\mathbb{R} \times X \to X, (λ,x)↦λx(\lambda, x) \mapsto \lambda x, where ℝ\mathbb{R} has the Euclidean topology, such that these operations together satisfy the axioms of a real vector space.

Some others require separation axioms like T2T_2 or T1T_1, though we do not.

Meta-properties

  • This property is preserved by arbitrary products.
  • This property is preserved by Σ\Sigma-products.

P000239Semilocally contractiblePredicate

Every point x∈Xx \in X has a neighborhood (equivalently, an open neighborhood) UU that is contractible in XX; i.e., such that the inclusion map U↪XU \hookrightarrow X is a null-homotopy.

Equivalently, every point x∈Xx \in X has a neighborhood (equivalently, an open neighborhood) UU of xx such that the inclusion map U↪XU \hookrightarrow X is homotopic to the constant map with value xx.

Defined as "weakly locally contractible" and given the acronym "wlc" in On fiber spaces (Fadell). Defined as "semi-locally contractible" in A characterization of local equi-connectedness (Sakai).

Meta-properties

  • This property is hereditary with respect to clopen sets.
  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is preserved by arbitrary disjoint unions.
  • This property is preserved by finite products.
  • If each point has a neighborhood with the property, XX also has the property.

P000240CW complexPredicate

XX has a chain of subspaces ∅=X−1⊆X0⊆X1⊆…\empty = X_{-1}\subseteq X_0\subseteq X_1 \subseteq \dots, such that:

  • XnX_n is obtained from Xn−1X_{n-1} by attaching nn-cells.
  • X=⋃n≥0XnX = \bigcup_{n\geq 0} X_n and a subspace U⊆XU \subseteq X is open iff U∩XnU \cap X_n open in XnX_n for all n≥−1n \geq -1.

Here attaching nn-cells means that there is a discrete space JJ, and for every j∈Jj \in J a continuous map fj:∂Dn→Xn−1f_j:\partial D^n \to X_{n-1}, such that XnX_n is homeomorphic to the quotient (Xn−1⊔(J×Dn))/∼(X_{n-1} \sqcup (J \times D^n)) /{\sim}, where ∼\sim is the equivalence relation generated by (j,x)∼fj(x)(j,x) \sim f_j(x) for all (j,x)∈J×∂Dn(j,x)\in J \times \partial D^n. The set JJ is allowed to be empty, in which case Xn=Xn−1X_n=X_{n-1}. The 00-skeleton X0X_0 has the discrete topology; if it is empty, XX itself is empty.

Here DnD^n is the closed unit disk in ℝn\mathbb R^n and ∂Dn=Sn−1\partial D^n=S^{n-1} is the unit sphere in ℝn\mathbb R^n. We set ∂D0=S−1=∅\partial D^0=S^{-1}=\emptyset by convention.

Note: A CW structure on a topological space XX is a filtration ∅=X−1⊆X0⊆X1⊆…\emptyset = X_{-1}\subseteq X_0\subseteq X_1 \subseteq\dots satisfying the conditions above. Strictly speaking, a CW complex is a space XX together with a compatible CW structure. For simplicity and by a slight abuse of language, we call the space itself a CW complex if it admits a CW structure.

Defined on page 5 of Algebraic Topology (Hatcher), also given in Theorem II.2.4 of The Topology of CW Complexes (Lundell & Weingram). See also https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/CW+complex.

An equivalent definition can be given in terms of a decomposition of XX into cells and conditions on their associated characteristic maps. For details and the meaning of this terminology, see Proposition A.2 on page 521 of Algebraic Topology (Hatcher) or Definition II.1.1 in The Topology of CW Complexes (Lundell & Weingram).

Meta-properties

  • This property is preserved by arbitrary disjoint unions.

P000241Locally a Euclidean half-linePredicate

Each point has a (not necessarily open) neighborhood homeomorphic to the closed half-line ℝ≥0\mathbb R_{\ge 0}, also homeomorphic to Interval [0,1)[0,1).

This is the special case of Locally an nn-Euclidean half-space with n=1n=1.

  • pp has an open neighborhood homeomorphic to Euclidean real numbers ℝ\mathbb R;
  • pp has an open neighborhood homeomorphic to Interval [0,1)[0,1) with pp mapped to the element 0∈[0,1)0\in[0,1).

P000242Weakly contractiblePredicate

XX is nonempty and for each integer n≥0n\ge 0 every continuous map Sn→XS^n\to X is homotopic to a constant map.

Equivalently, XX is nonempty, Path connected and all homotopy groups πn(X)\pi_n(X) with n≥1n\ge 1 are trivial. In other words, XX is weakly homotopy equivalent to The Singleton.

Notation above: SnS^n is the unit sphere in ℝn+1\mathbb R^{n+1}.

Defined as weakly contractible for example on page 2 in On the universal space for group actions with compact isotropy (Lück, Meintrup) (accessible here). Defined as homotopically trivial on page 281 of A stronger reformulation of Webb’s conjecture in terms of finite topological spaces (Piterman). Borsuk uses the terminology C∞C^\infty, defined as XX being nn-connected for all n≥0n\ge 0 (see page 30 of Theory of retracts (Borsuk)).

Meta-properties

  • This property is preserved by arbitrary products (see Proposition 4.2 in Algebraic Topology (Hatcher)).
  • This property is preserved by homotopy equivalences.

P000243Has countable π\pi-weightPredicate

XX has a countable π\pi-base.

A π\pi-base for XX is a collection 𝒱\mathcal{V} of nonempty open sets in XX such that every nonempty open U⊆XU\subseteq X contains some V∈𝒱V\in\mathcal V.

Such a space has countable π\pi-weight, where the π\pi-weight is defined as

πw(X):=min⁡{∣𝒱∣:𝒱 is a π-base for X}+ω.\quad\quad\pi w(X):=\min\{|\mathcal V|:\mathcal V \text{ is a }\pi\text{-base for }X\}+\omega.

Defined on page 14 of Cardinal functions I (R. Hodel), Ch. 1 of Handbook of set-theoretic topology.

Meta-properties

  • This property is hereditary with respect to dense sets.
  • This property is hereditary with respect to open sets.
  • If some open dense subset of XX has the property, then so does XX.
  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol⁡(X)\operatorname{Kol}(X) does.
  • This property is preserved by countable products.
  • This property is preserved by countable disjoint unions.

P000244Has countable π\pi-characterPredicate

Every point in XX has a countable local π\pi-base.

A local π\pi-base for x∈Xx \in X is a collection 𝒱x\mathcal{V}_x of nonempty open sets in XX such that every neighbourhood UU of xx contains some V∈𝒱xV \in \mathcal V_x. (Note: We don't require that x∈Vx \in V, i.e., the elements of 𝒱x\mathcal{V}_x need not be neighbourhoods of xx.)

Such a space has countable π\pi-character, where the π\pi-character is defined as

πχ(X):=sup⁡{πχ(x,X):x∈X}+ω\quad\quad\pi\chi(X):=\sup\{\pi\chi(x,X):x\in X\}+\omega

with πχ(x,X)\pi\chi(x,X) being the minimum size of a local π\pi-base for xx.

Defined on page 16 of Cardinal functions I (R. Hodel), Ch. 1 of Handbook of set-theoretic topology.

P000247Has connected quasicomponentsPredicate

Every quasicomponent of XX is connected. That is, quasicomponents and connected components coincide.

Equivalently, any two distinct connected components AA and BB of XX can be separated by clopen sets (i.e., A⊆UA\subseteq U and B⊆X∖UB\subseteq X\setminus U for some clopen set UU).

The quasicomponent of a point x∈Xx\in X is the intersection of all clopen sets containing xx. It is the set of points y∈Xy\in X that cannot be separated from xx by a clopen set. See definition on p. 356 of General Topology (Engelking, 1989).

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
  • An arbitrary product of nonempty spaces satisfies this property iff each of its factors does.[1]^{[1]}

[1] use: the quasicomponents are products of quasicomponents in each factor; see The equivalence relation induced by the partition into quasi-components is multiplicative.

P000248FF-spacePredicate

Any two disjoint cozero sets are contained in disjoint zero sets.

Equivalently, every cozero set is C∗C^\ast-embedded.

See Theorem 14.25 in Rings of Continuous Functions (Gillman & Jerison) for more equivalent characterizations, of which many hold without the T312T_{3 \frac{1}{2}} condition which is assumed throughout that book.

Note: XX is an FF-space iff Tych(X)\text{Tych}(X) is an FF-space, where Tych(X)\text{Tych}(X) is the Tychonoff reflection of XX (see for example Cozero complemented property for a space and its Tychonoff reflection).

Originally introduced for T312T_{3 \frac{1}{2}} spaces in Definition 2.1 of Rings of continuous functions in which every finitely generated ideal is principal (Gillman & Henriksen). Here we do not assume T312T_{3 \frac{1}{2}}.

Terminology: A set Z⊆XZ\subseteq X is a zero set if there exists a continuous function f:X→ℝf:X\to\mathbb{R} such that Z=f−1(0)Z = f^{-1}(0). A cozero set is the complement of a zero set. A set A⊆XA\subseteq X is C∗C^\ast-embedded if every bounded continuous function A→ℝA\to\mathbb{R} extends to a continuous function on XX.

Meta-properties

  • XX satisfies this property iff its Kolmogorov quotient Kol(X)\text{Kol}(X) does.
